## Statement

Synthetic data generation trains a generative model on available individual patient data and emits artificial patient records that reproduce the source demographics, baseline characteristics and outcomes; it is now being proposed as an indirect-comparison route, carrying a claim of greater precision than MAIC where population overlap is poor. Nothing establishes what such a comparison identifies. Three questions have no answer: whether an apparent precision gain reflects information or the smoothing and extrapolation behavior of the generator, what the estimand is when synthetic records are compared against a real comparator arm, and how generator uncertainty propagates into the reported interval. The evidence base is thinner than the proposal: the precision claim is reported in a conference abstract, and the peer-reviewed review that repeats it states in print that validation evidence remains limited and that no comprehensive simulation studies have systematically assessed performance across a range of realistic rare-disease settings. No study scores the route across overlap, sample size and covariate-type regimes against MAIC, simulated treatment comparison and multilevel network meta-regression, and no reporting standard specifies which generator, which training data, and which fidelity and disclosure diagnostics must accompany a submission. The substantial adjacent literature on synthetic clinical trial data evaluates distributional fidelity, analytic utility and privacy risk; none of it addresses what a treatment contrast built on synthetic records means.

## Why it is open

The claimed advantage lies exactly where the underlying data carry least information: poor overlap means few real patients resemble the target, so whatever the generator supplies in that region is model output rather than evidence, and separating the two requires a truth that the applied setting does not have. There is no estimand to check against either, because a generative model reproduces a joint distribution rather than a causal contrast, so the target quantity has to be imposed by whoever specifies the comparison and none of the current proposals does so. Uncertainty propagation is a further unresolved layer, since the generator is fitted, sampled from and then analyzed, and no published route carries fit uncertainty and synthetic sampling variability through to the interval. Evaluation also falls between two fields: the synthetic-data literature scores fidelity, utility and disclosure risk with no consensus metric and with most studies underestimating privacy risk, while the population-adjustment literature scores bias, coverage and mean squared error against a known truth, and the crossed evaluation this route needs has not been built. The work exists mainly as conference abstracts from a single group, so there is no full specification for anyone else to reproduce or refute.

## What has been tried

::: {.table-scroll}

| Work | What it contributes |
|---|---|
| [Parkitny et al. 2026, Journal of Market Access and Health Policy](https://doi.org/10.3390/jmahp14010014) | Reviews population-adjusted indirect comparison in rare disease; treats synthetic data generation as an experimental extension, repeats the precision claim from a conference abstract, and states that no comprehensive simulation studies have systematically assessed its performance across realistic rare-disease settings. |
| [Aballea et al. 2024, Value in Health (ISPOR abstract MSR127)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jval.2024.10.2361) | Proposes synthetic data generation as a route to population-adjusted indirect comparison with an applied case in diabetic macular edema; the origin of the greater-precision-than-MAIC claim, published as a conference abstract. |
| [Aballea et al. 2025, Value in Health (ISPOR abstract PT27)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jval.2025.09.3505) | Assesses the performance of the synthetic-data route against simulated treatment comparison for unanchored indirect comparison; the nearest thing to a benchmark, covering one comparator method and available only as an abstract. |
| [Elvatun et al. 2025, PLOS Digital Health](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pdig.0000581) | Uses synthetic data as external control arms for scarce single-arm trials; the closest published relative, framed as external control rather than as indirect comparison, and inheriting the unanchored identification problem in full. |
| [El Emam, Mosquera and Zheng 2021, JAMIA](https://doi.org/10.1093/jamia/ocaa249) | Sequential-tree synthesis of clinical trial datasets with the variable order optimized against utility metrics; the generator technology being proposed, evaluated on distributional fidelity rather than against any causal target. |
| [El Kababji et al. 2023, JCO Clinical Cancer Informatics](https://doi.org/10.1200/CCI.23.00116) | Compares sequential synthesis, conditional GAN and variational autoencoder on eight breast cancer trials, replicating published analyses and measuring attribution and membership disclosure risk; shows what a careful synthetic-data evaluation covers and what it leaves out. |
| [Kaabachi et al. 2025, npj Digital Medicine](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41746-024-01359-3) | Scoping review of privacy and utility metrics for medical synthetic data; finds no consensus metric and that most studies underestimate privacy risk, so there is no ready-made scoring rule to borrow. |
| [Yan et al. 2022, Nature Communications](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-35295-1) | Multifaceted benchmarking of synthetic health record generation models, establishing that no generator dominates across utility and privacy and that performance is task-dependent. |
| [Pasculli et al. 2025, CPT: Pharmacometrics and Systems Pharmacology](https://doi.org/10.1002/psp4.70021) | Surveys definitions, regulatory frameworks and open issues for synthetic data in healthcare and drug development; the closest thing to a regulatory framing, since no agency has issued a position paper on synthetic evidence generation. |
| [Remiro-Azocar, Heath and Baio 2022, Research Synthesis Methods](https://doi.org/10.1002/jrsm.1565) | Parametric G-computation for indirect comparison, which also simulates pseudo-patients but from a specified covariate model inside a declared estimand; the disciplined comparator a generative route should be scored against. |
| [Remiro-Azocar, Heath and Baio 2021, Research Synthesis Methods](https://doi.org/10.1002/jrsm.1511) | Review and simulation study of population-adjustment methods whose factor grid over overlap, sample size and covariate structure is the standard against which any new route is evaluated. |

:::

## Probable solution or research direction

Define what a synthetic-data comparison identifies before scoring it: write the target as a marginal or conditional contrast in a declared population, then say which step of generate-then-analyze carries the identification, since a generator that reproduces a joint distribution supplies no causal content on its own. Score generator families against known truth on the standard population-adjustment factor grid, crossing overlap, sample size, covariate type and the strength of effect modification, with MAIC, simulated treatment comparison and multilevel network meta-regression as references and with mean squared error, coverage and interval width reported together, so that a precision gain accompanied by undercoverage is visible as such. Separate information from smoothing directly by holding the real data fixed and varying only the generator's flexibility and its behavior outside the observed support. Build the uncertainty route, since an honest interval must carry generator fit uncertainty, synthetic sampling variability and outcome-model uncertainty; the natural candidates are a Bayesian generative model propagated through posterior predictive draws, or a bootstrap that refits the generator at every replicate. Write the reporting requirement in the same pass: generator family and hyperparameters, training data and provenance, number of synthetic records, fidelity and disclosure diagnostics, and a demonstration that the analysis reproduces the source-trial result when applied to synthetic records drawn from the source itself.

## Verification

::: {.verification-trail}
**Verdict.** Confirmed open. One reader proposed this from a single 2026 review, and the reviewer accepted it on the grounds that generating substitute patient records is not the same as using a flexible nuisance or outcome model inside a conventional population-adjusted comparison. An independent search of the literature confirms the thinness rather than merely the novelty: the route exists as conference abstracts from one group, the precision claim traces to a single abstract, and the peer-reviewed review states in print that no comprehensive simulation study of its performance exists.

:::
